strengths: The paper explores an underexplored direction in learned optimization: integrating learnable components into second-order (quasi-Newton, specifically SR1) methods, rather than the dominant first-order learned optimizers.

The design is principled: the preconditioner is structured as B_0 + sum v_i v_i^T, guaranteeing positive semi-definiteness by construction, and the secant condition is encouraged via a differentiable penalty (secant loss) folded into the meta-training objective, which adds no inference-time overhead.

The architecture is dimension-invariant (element-wise MLPs), and the experiments genuinely probe cross-dimension generalization (meta-training on N=2 quadratics, testing at N=10 up to N=1000), which is a meaningful robustness test for learned optimizers.

The method is validated on both analytic benchmarks (quadratics, Rosenbrock, Rastrigin with performance profiles following standard methodology) and a real application (HMR), where it replaces the LGD update module of Song et al. [54] and achieves better PA-MPJPE (51.58 vs 55.90) with fewer parameters (10.4M vs 17.4M) and faster per-iteration runtime (91ms vs 166ms).

Good reproducibility practices: detailed hyperparameter tables (Table 6), full MLP architectures, data generation protocols, ablations over hidden dimensions and encoder inputs (Table 3), and compute/memory analysis (Figs. 6-7, Table 2). Code release is promised.
An honest limitations appendix is included, acknowledging higher runtime relative to first-order methods.
weaknesses: The central 'learned projection' framing is somewhat overstated: Eq. (6)/(8) define a hard projection onto PSD-structured matrices satisfying the secant condition, but in practice the secant condition is only softly enforced through a weighted penalty (lambda_sec) in the meta-loss (Eq. 9). PSD-ness is guaranteed trivially by the v v^T structure (already noted for [17]), so the actual novelty and behavior of the projection mechanism deserves more careful characterization, including sensitivity to lambda_sec, which is not analyzed.

There is no theoretical treatment of the learned method at all. Claims in the conclusions such as 'converging to the global minimum faster' are unsupported, particularly for the non-convex benchmark functions where global convergence is not established.

The evidence base for generalization is narrow: meta-training is on quadratics (N=2), Rosenbrock, and Rastrigin only, and evaluation uses the same function families. There are no experiments on more realistic optimization problems for learned optimizers (e.g., training neural networks, MLP-MNIST style tasks), which limits claims about broad usefulness of the optimizer.

The HMR evaluation is limited to a single framework (LGD [54]) and a single dataset (3DPW), with essentially one learned-optimization baseline. The claim of 'state-of-the-art' performance should be qualified: it is SOTA only within the narrow optimization-based/self-supervised HMR setting, and no statistical significance or variance is reported for the 51.58 vs 55.90 improvement.

Some technical inconsistencies: p_k is defined as x_k - x_{k-1} in Sec. 3.2 but as x_{k+1} - x_k in Appendix F.2; Lemma 1 is trivial and its 'proof' formatting is broken. Figures 1 and 3 are small and hard to read, making visual claims about trajectory and profile comparisons difficult to verify.

The learned learning-rate generator introduces extra hyperparameters (gamma_1, gamma_2) and buffer sizes differ between train and test (e.g., L=16 train, L=64 test in Table 6); the effect of these choices and the fairness of baseline step-size tuning deserve more discussion.

The relation to prior second-order learned optimizers (Q-Newton of Li & Malik [29], Gartner et al. [17], Ayad et al. [5]) is discussed only qualitatively; no empirical comparison against any of them is provided, making it hard to gauge the practical advance over existing learned second-order approaches.

strengths: The core idea—integrating a learned preconditioning unit into the classical SR1 framework while preserving Quasi-Newton structure (secant condition, PSD) via a differentiable penalty—is sensible and sits in a relatively underexplored corner of learned optimization (learned second-order methods).

The method is lightweight and dimension-invariant by design (element-wise MLPs), which is a practical advantage over heavy learned optimizers, and the HMR results (Table 1: 51.58 PA-MPJPE vs. 55.90 for LGD, with fewer parameters, 10.4M vs. 17.4M) and runtime/memory comparisons (Table 2) are concrete and non-trivial.

The evaluation includes standard tools from the optimization literature (performance profiles, cosine similarity to the Newton direction), the ablations in Appendix B justify architectural choices, and the paper is generally clearly written with a reasonable limitations discussion.
The approach is self-supervised and requires no annotated data or fine-tuning for the target task, which is an appealing property for integration into optimization-based pipelines.
weaknesses: Novelty is overstated. The central construction—a preconditioner built as a sum of learned vector outer products v_i v_i^T, which guarantees PSD by construction—is explicitly acknowledged to follow prior learned optimizers (Gartner et al. [17]). The claimed 'learned projection' (Eq. 6-8) is not actually computed as a projection; it is a soft secant penalty added to the meta-loss (Eq. 9). The paper conflates a hard constrained optimization problem (Eq. 6, 8) with a penalized training objective, and no analysis is given of how well the penalty enforces the secant condition at inference time.

No theoretical grounding for the learned method. Classical SR1 has known convergence properties; L-SR1 has none. There is no analysis of stability, behavior of the learned step sizes, or guarantees that the descent direction property (Lemma 1) holds when the secant penalty is only approximately satisfied. Lemma 1 itself is a textbook result about PSD matrices, not about the proposed method.

The empirical scope is narrow. Analytic experiments are limited to quadratics (trained at N=2, tested at N=10), Rosenbrock, and Rastrigin, with a single test set of 30 problems. Critically, there are no comparisons against strong modern learned optimizers (e.g., VeLO, learned Adam variants, or the second-order-inspired baselines the paper itself cites like Li et al. [29] and Ayad et al. [5]), which is essential to substantiate the claim that this is a better way to fuse learning with second-order methods.

The HMR evaluation compares only against LGD (2020) and SMPLify, and does not compare against the recent deep regression/refinement HMR methods the paper itself discusses (e.g., PromptHMR [64], PIP [49]). The claim of 'state-of-the-art performance with a notably compact model' in the abstract is therefore not substantiated against the actual state of the art.

Reproducibility is weak at submission time: code is only promised ('Code will be made publicly available'), several key details are deferred to unavailable supplementary material, and meta-training requires ~15 hours on an RTX 3090 plus careful hyperparameter tuning (Table 6), making independent verification difficult without the code.

Presentation of evidence has gaps: Figure 3a shows only the first 20 update steps, making long-horizon behavior on quadratics unclear (L-SR1 curves appear to flatten above LBFGS); error bars/confidence intervals are absent from the analytic experiments; and the performance profile in Fig. 3c lumps heterogeneous problem families without per-family breakdowns.

Practicality claims are partially contradicted by the results: the limitations section concedes high runtime relative to first-order methods (Fig. 6), and in the HMR task L-SR1 needs 13 steps to reach its best error versus 4 for LGD (Table 1), so the end-to-end wall-clock advantage over the baseline it improves upon is not clearly established.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored direction: learned second-order (Quasi-Newton) optimizers, whereas most learned optimization work targets first-order methods. This is a meaningful gap identified in the related work section.

The design is principled: the structured PSD form of Eq. (7) (sum of outer products plus B0 = I) guarantees positive semi-definiteness by construction, while the secant penalty in the meta-loss (Eq. 9) softly encourages the classical SR1 constraint, preserving interpretable Quasi-Newton structure within a learned architecture.
The element-wise MLP design provides dimension invariance, and this is empirically validated (meta-training on N=2, testing on N=10 for quadratics; testing up to N=1000 in performance profiles).

Evaluation covers both analytic benchmarks (quadratics with controlled conditioning, Rosenbrock, Rastrigin) and a real application (HMR on 3DPW), with cosine-similarity-to-Newton-direction analysis (Fig. 3b) that mechanistically supports the claim that the projection improves curvature alignment.

Supplementary material is thorough: computational/runtime/memory analysis (Appendix A), ablations on encoder inputs and hidden dimension (Table 3), full architecture and hyperparameter details (Appendix C), and an honest limitations discussion (Appendix D) noting the higher runtime relative to first-order methods.

The HMR result is practically relevant: better PA-MPJPE (51.58 vs 55.90) than LGD [54] with fewer parameters (10.4M vs 17.4M) and roughly half the per-iteration runtime (Table 2), without requiring fine-tuning or annotated optimization data.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'enforcing' the secant condition is overstated. Eq. (6) formulates a hard projection, but the implementation is a soft penalty (Eq. 8-9) added to the meta-loss; PSD is guaranteed structurally, but secant satisfaction is only encouraged, not enforced. The paper should be more precise about this distinction.

The empirical scope is narrow for a learned optimizer paper. There are no experiments optimizing neural networks or other machine learning objectives—the canonical testbed for learned optimizers (e.g., learned optimizers evaluated on MNIST/CIFAR training). Generalization claims rest on synthetic functions and one vision task.

The HMR comparison is limited to LGD [54]. Other learned optimization-based HMR methods cited in the paper (e.g., [26], [49]) are not compared against, and 'outperforms existing learned optimization-based approaches' is not substantiated beyond a single baseline. Only one evaluation dataset (3DPW) is used; standard benchmarks like 3DOH or EB, or in-distribution AMASS evaluation, are absent.

The performance profile setup raises a generalization question: separate models are meta-trained per task (quadratics, Rosenbrock, Rastrigin; Table 6), yet the test suite mixes all task types. It is unclear which checkpoint is evaluated on the mixed test set, and the claim of a 'single optimizer generalizing across tasks' is not cleanly demonstrated.

Statistical rigor is thin: test sets are small (30 problems, 32 functions), and no variance, confidence intervals, or repeated seeds are reported for the headline results (Table 1, Fig. 3c). The HMR improvement (55.90 to 51.58), while consistent with Fig. 4, is not accompanied by significance analysis.
The L-SR1 needs more steps than LGD to reach its best error (13 vs 4 in Table 1), somewhat tempering the convergence-speed narrative; the trade-off is discussed only implicitly.

No convergence theory is provided for the learned variant (understandable for learned optimizers, but a brief discussion of what guarantees do and do not carry over from SR1 would strengthen the paper).

Code availability is promised ('will be made publicly available') but not provided at review time, which limits reproducibility of the meta-training pipeline given its sensitivity to hyperparameters (e.g., λ_sec = 100 vs 1 across experiments).

strengths: Well-motivated integration of learned components into a principled quasi-Newton (SR1) structure, with a clear positioning against prior learned second-order work (Li et al. 2020, Gärtner et al. 2023, Liao et al. 2023).

The PGSM design is clean: PSD-by-construction rank-one parameterization plus a secant-violation penalty during meta-training, avoiding an explicit projection subproblem at inference. The authors honestly acknowledge (Sec. 3.2/p.4) that the composite update with element-wise learning rates does not guarantee descent, which is a commendably honest treatment rather than an overclaim.

Thorough controlled evaluation: effect of PGSM vs. no projection (Figs. 3a/3b), generalization from N=2 to N=10 without retraining (App. B.1), buffer-size robustness sweeps (Fig. 3c), performance profiles on a 30-problem suite (Fig. 4), module/input ablations (App. B.3), scalar vs. vector learning-rate ablation with separately meta-trained checkpoints (App. B.2), and a data-efficiency study (Table 5).

Real-world demonstration on HMR: L-SR1 outperforms LGD (55.90 → 51.58 PA-MPJPE) with a smaller model (10.4M vs 17.4M params), lower per-iteration cost (91ms vs 166ms), and faster wall-clock at matched horizons; the secant-penalty analysis at inference (Fig. 7) nicely connects the training objective to test-time behavior.
Reasonable reproducibility: detailed architectures, hyperparameters for all experiments (Tables 6-8), runtime/memory breakdowns (App. A), and a project page with code.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is incremental. Replacing the SR1 denominator update with learned PSD rank-one vectors and adding a secant penalty to the meta-loss is a fairly simple modification; the machinery (element-wise MLP modules, log-learning-rate parameterization) closely follows Gärtner et al. (2023) and Metz et al. (2022), and the paper itself concedes this lineage.

No comparison against other learned second-order optimizers on the analytic benchmarks: performance profiles compare only to L-BFGS, Adam, and AdaHessian, while the most relevant learned baselines (Gärtner et al., Liao et al., Li et al.) appear only as citations. On HMR the only learned baseline is LGD. This weakens the claim of 'state-of-the-art' performance among learned optimizers.

The 'no task-specific fine-tuning' claim needs qualification: the HMR optimizer is meta-trained specifically on AMASS with the Song et al. framework, and performance-profile models are each meta-trained separately per objective family (quadratics, Rosenbrock, Rastrigin). Generalization is shown across dimensions and buffer sizes, but not convincingly across task families.

No convergence or stability theory is provided; Lemma F.1 is a trivial textbook statement, and the descent-property caveat is left to empirical validation. The usefulness of the PSD-by-construction argument is therefore weaker than the framing suggests.

Absolute positioning is limited: on 3DPW, regression-based methods (WHAM 35.9, PromptHMR 36.6) substantially outperform all optimization-based methods including L-SR1 (51.58), so the practical significance is confined to the optimization-based, data-scarce regime; the paper's own limitations section appropriately scopes this, but the contribution remains specialized.

Minor presentation issues: the Table 3 sign convention (negative scalar-row losses vs. positive vector-row losses) is confusing without explanation; Fig. 3a legends are illegibly cluttered; inconsistent notation (γ2 vs. γ) across Sec. 4.1 and App. C.2; and meta-training cost (15h on one GPU; 400K iterations for HMR) makes 'data-efficient' claims relative only to the downstream regression alternative.

strengths: The PGSM idea is a reasonable synthesis: enforcing PSD-by-construction rank-one preconditioners while penalizing secant violation only during meta-training avoids an inference-time projection, and the paper is transparent that the composite operator (element-wise learning rates applied to a PSD direction) forfeits formal descent guarantees (Section 3.2 discussion).

The experimental design includes a number of useful controlled ablations: buffer-size robustness at train/test time (Fig. 3c), encoder-input and hidden-dimension sweeps (Table 4), element-wise vs. scalarized learning rates with separate meta-trained checkpoints (Table 3), limited-data HMR training (Table 5), and computational cost breakdowns (Figs. 8-9, Table 2).

The method is dimension-invariant by construction (element-wise MLPs with shared parameters), which is a sensible design for learned optimizers, and per-iteration costs of 91ms/10.4M params compare favorably against LGD (166ms/17.4M params) on HMR.

The limitations appendix (Appendix D) is honest, acknowledging the higher per-step cost relative to first-order methods, task-distribution-specific meta-training, and added hyperparameters (buffer size, unroll depth, λsec).
weaknesses: The central 'second-order/curvature-aware' claim is weakly supported. The constructed preconditioner B̃k = B0 + Σ vivi⊤ does not satisfy the secant condition — the paper concedes this and substitutes only a soft penalty during meta-training. The result is arguably a learned diagonal-scaled PSD preconditioner rather than a genuine quasi-Newton method; the key structural property distinguishing SR1 (exact secant satisfaction) is precisely what is lost. No analysis is offered of when the penalty converges to actual secant satisfaction or how far the learned matrices are from secant solutions.

In the controlled quadratic setting where claims should be strongest, L-BFGS outperforms L-SR1 (the paper admits LBFGS 'exhibits the fastest convergence across all tested settings', Fig. 3a). L-SR1 only beats its own no-PGSM ablation; the improvement over classical baselines comes only from the heterogeneous performance-profile aggregate (Fig. 4), and no learned-optimizer baselines (e.g., Gärtner et al. 2023, VeLO, Liao et al. 2023) are included there despite being cited as closest related work.

The generalization-across-dimensions evidence is underwhelming and spun favorably: models trained at N=2 evaluated at N=10 show worse AUC (3.07 vs. 7.33), and the claim reduces to 'hyperparameter rankings are preserved.' Moreover, because all modules are element-wise MLPs with no cross-coordinate mixing, it is conceptually unclear how off-diagonal curvature structure — the essence of second-order information — can ever be learned; the paper does not address this tension.

The HMR comparison set is narrow: the only learned-optimization baseline is LGD (Song et al., 2020) from 2020, and the accuracy gain (51.58 vs. 55.90 PA-MPJPE) is modest while remaining far behind modern regression methods (WHAM 35.9), acknowledged only via training-scope caveats. The headline 'state-of-the-art performance' is therefore an overclaim relative to the evidence.

Fig. 5b (PA-MPJPE vs. inner iterations) shows L-SR1 plateauing and slightly degrading after iteration ~9, while LBFGS continues to improve; the fixed-horizon narrative obscures this. The 4-step vs. full-horizon reporting also complicates comparison of convergence-speed claims.

Ablation results raise unexplained inconsistencies: on quadratics the scalarized learning rate achieves lower loss (-2.27 vs. 3.07 in Table 3), yet element-wise is adopted as the default with only a 0.22mm HMR gain as justification. The λsec hyperparameter sweep appears only in appendix heatmaps, and no ablation isolates the learning-rate generator's contribution on HMR.

No theoretical grounding for stability or convergence of the learned scheme is provided; behavior is justified entirely empirically, which is a notable gap for a paper whose central contribution is a structural modification to a quasi-Newton method.

Reproducibility is mixed: code is promised ('Project page and code:' is left as an empty reference), and many details (seeds for HMR, variance on 3DPW results, line-search handling for LBFGS in Fig. 5) are absent or deferred.

strengths: Novel and sensible combination of learned optimization with quasi-Newton structure: the PSD-by-construction rank-one parameterization (outer products of learned vectors) avoids expensive projection subproblems at inference while the meta-training secant penalty encourages approximate secant consistency, preserving interpretability in the model-based deep learning paradigm.

The PGSM ablation is convincing in a controlled setting: on quadratic objectives the variant with the secant penalty consistently outperforms the No-Prj variant in both convergence (Fig. 3a) and alignment with the Newton direction (Fig. 3b), directly supporting the claimed role of the secant penalty.

Thorough analytic study: dimension generalization heatmaps (App. B.1), buffer-size robustness (Fig. 3c), learning-rate scalarization comparison (App. B.2, with a separate end-to-end meta-trained scalarized checkpoint rather than a post-hoc freeze), encoder-input and hidden-dimension ablations (App. B.3), and data-efficiency experiments (App. B.4, Table 5).

Practically useful HMR results: L-SR1 outperforms LGD in PA-MPJPE (51.74 vs. 55.90 at a 4-step horizon) with fewer parameters (10.4M vs. 17.4M), less runtime (91 vs. 166 ms/iteration), and no task-specific fine-tuning; the pose-block secant penalty analysis (Fig. 7) provides evidence that PGSM training transfers to the downstream task.

Honest and specific limitations section (App. D) acknowledging higher per-step cost than first-order methods, task-distribution dependence of meta-training, and added hyperparameters; runtime/memory breakdowns are provided (App. A), and code is promised via a project page.
The paper is candid that the PSD-based descent intuition does not extend to the composite map with coordinate-wise learning rates (Sec. 3.2), avoiding overclaiming theoretical guarantees.
weaknesses: Key learned second-order baselines are missing from the comparisons. The related-work section discusses Gärtner et al. (2023) and Liao et al. (2023) at length, but neither (nor VeLO) appears in the performance-profile benchmark or HMR evaluation; the main learned baseline is LGD (2020). This weakens the central claim of outperforming learned second-order optimizers.

The headline absolute advantage over classical solvers is modest and setting-dependent: L-BFGS converges fastest on the controlled quadratic experiments (Sec. 5.1.1 admits this), and the performance-profile gain in Fig. 4 over tuned L-BFGS/Adam/AdaHessian appears small; no numerical margins or statistical treatment are reported for the profile comparison.

Generalization-across-dimension claims are overstated relative to the evidence: absolute AUC worsens substantially at N=10 vs. N=2 (3.07 vs. 7.33), and the supported claim is only that hyperparameter rankings are preserved; the introduction's claim that the optimizer 'generalizes across problem sizes without re-training' reads stronger than what is demonstrated.

The 'state-of-the-art' phrasing is scope-limited (optimization-based, AMASS-only); regression methods such as WHAM (35.9) and PromptHMR (36.6) substantially outperform L-SR1 (51.58) on 3DPW. The paper frames this correctly in Table 1, but the abstract/introduction language could mislead.

Theoretical support is thin: the learned vectors v_k are unconstrained at inference, so secant satisfaction and PSD-based descent behavior are purely empirical; the secant penalty is only motivated by (not equivalent to) the PSD projection, and no convergence or stability analysis of the learned update is attempted.

Hyperparameter sensitivity of the secant weight (λsec = 100 for quadratics vs. 1–10 elsewhere; Table 8) is not analyzed, leaving reproducibility of the tuning protocol somewhat uncertain; some presentation issues remain (e.g., inconsistent gamma notation in App. C, mixed w/o sec./No Prj. labeling).
